title: Uttarakhand Bans Gutkha, Pan Masala and All Tobacco Food Products for One Year
excerpt: The order by Food Safety and Drug Administration Commissioner Vinay Pandey covers manufacture, storage, distribution and sale. It renews a line of state bans going back to 2013 — in a country where a Lancet Global Health study links chewing tobacco to roughly 251,000 deaths worldwide in 2023, 84% of them in South Asia.
body:
• Uttarakhand has imposed a one-year ban on the manufacture, storage, distribution and sale of gutkha, pan masala and other food products containing tobacco or nicotine.
  • The order was issued by Food Safety and Drug Administration Commissioner Vinay Pandey, citing public health concerns.
  • The legal basis is the national food-safety rule that tobacco and nicotine cannot be used as ingredients in any food product — the same basis states have used since 2012.
  • The health stakes are quantified in a recent Lancet Global Health study: chewing tobacco contributed to about 251,000 deaths worldwide in 2023, with South Asia accounting for roughly 84% of the burden.

Uttarakhand has banned gutkha, pan masala and every other food product containing tobacco or nicotine for one year, in an order covering manufacture, storage, distribution and sale across the state. Food Safety and Drug Administration Commissioner Vinay Pandey issued the order citing public health concerns. Uttarakhand has walked this road before — similar bans were imposed in 2013, 2015 and 2019 — because the underlying national rule is permanent but state orders enforcing it are time-bound and must be renewed.

The law behind the ban

The foundation is a 2011 ruling by India's food safety regulator, FSSAI, that tobacco and nicotine cannot be used as an ingredient in any food product. Because gutkha is sold as a food product, that single rule became the legal base for state bans from 2012 onward; in time every state and Union Territory had one. The Uttarakhand order therefore does not create a new prohibition so much as reactivate enforcement machinery — inspections, seizures and penalties — for another twelve months.

Why bans on paper have not ended gutkha

The honest context for any new ban is the record of the old ones, examined in a recent analysis of why India's gutkha ban isn't working. Manufacturers adapted to the ingredient rule by splitting the product in two: pan masala sold without tobacco, and flavoured chewing tobacco sold alongside it, with the customer mixing the two on the spot. The Supreme Court noticed the device in 2016 and directed authorities to enforce the law against it; many states now write orders that also cover products sold separately but intended to be mixed. Even so, sachets remain easy to find in much of the country — evidence that the binding constraint is enforcement capacity, not legal wording.

What is at stake

The numbers explain why states keep trying. A study in The Lancet Global Health estimates chewing tobacco contributed to about 251,000 deaths worldwide in 2023, with South Asia accounting for roughly 84 per cent of them; India is among the ten countries carrying more than 90 per cent of the global burden. Oral cancer alone kills over 70,000 Indians a year by commonly cited estimates, many cases attributed to chewing tobacco. Against that background, Uttarakhand's renewal is best judged not by its announcement but by what its food safety officers seize and prosecute over the next year — the measure every previous ban in the state, and the country, has ultimately been graded on.
